newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada decides not to back China rights resolution.
newsitem.headline: Canada decides not to back China rights resolution.

text.p: The Canadian government decided on Monday not to support a U.N. resolution critical of China's human rights record, arguing that bilateral committees and visits would be more effective.

Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said a key factor had been the decision by France, followed by several other Western nations, to stop co-sponsoring the annual resolution at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva.

"The government has decided, in light of the significant weakening in consensus on the resolution among its traditional co-sponsors, that it no longer carries the same weight it has in past years," he told a news conference.
"Under the circumstances, we concluded that Canada could have a greater influence on the state of human rights in China by pursuing and intensifying our promising bilateral measures."
The resolution was being sponsored by Denmark, the United States and 13 other countries.

Despite intense lobbying by Washington, support this year looks weak for the resolution, which has been defeated for six years in a row due to Third World support for China in the 61-member commission.
Canadian human rights activists charge that Liberal Prime Minister Jean Chretien has seemed more concerned with Canadian exports than human rights in his "constructive engagement" policy.
He has led two trade missions to China in which billions of dollars of deals were signed, including the sale of two nuclear reactors in a C$4 billion (U.S.$3 billion) deal.
Axworthy, widely viewed as more traditionally liberal than Chretien, said he did not raise trade matters in a visit to China in early April.
And he stated on Monday: "Canada remained very concerned about the state of human rights in China, particularly in the areas of religious freedoms and political dissent."
He listed several new "cooperative" Canada-China initiatives, including a joint committee on human rights.

It was not clear if this had been established as a result of Monday's decision to abandon the U.N. resolution, but he said China had made it clear that there was a linkage between the resolution and bilateral rights initiatives.
Canadian church leaders would also go to China this summer, and Canada would help train Chinese lawyers and educate Chinese police.

He also said China had agreed to support the signing of an agreement giving access by the International Committee of the Red Cross to Chinese prisoners, though he said this was not as the result of Canada's decision on the resolution.

The minister said he would be examining the situation to see if progress is made before deciding how to approach the resolution next year. "I think we all know that it was a tough judgment call to make," Axworthy said.
